content:
"The humid sting of the Darwin night did little to sober Dale Scott Walkinshaw, though the twisted metal of the Toyota Hilux wrapped around a palm tree near the airport was enough to startle him into a haze of adrenaline. For the officers pulling up to the corner of Stuart Highway and Bagot Road, the scene was chaotic: debris scattered like shrapnel, the smell of burnt rubber and leaking fuel heavy in the air. 

They found Walkinshaw crouching in the overgrown verge, cradling the passenger he had met only hours earlier at a bar. He was barely coherent, his blood-alcohol reading later clocking in at a staggering 0.149, miles past any limit of reason. Yet, the tragedy unfolding on that roadside was merely the prequel to a deeper, institutional failing. 

When the police took Walkinshaw into custody, placing him into the dark, metal containment of a caged van, they were ushering him into a system that had already been marked as lethal. The coroner’s subsequent findings would peel back layers of negligence that dated back years. Beneath the surface of that night’s police report—the arrest, the breathalyzer, the standard processing—lay the ghost of an internal warning ignored since 2013: a recommendation to install CCTV in those very vehicles to monitor for self-harm.

In the cavernous, unobserved space of that van, away from the eyes of the officers who had just pulled him from the crash, Walkinshaw disintegrated. He joined a grim, rising statistic. Between the previous death in custody and his own, sixteen others had attempted to end their lives in the same blind spots of police transport. In six of those instances, silence had proven deadly, with victims found only when their breath had all but faded.

For coroner Greg Cavanagh, the verdict was damning: the system hadn't just failed to prevent the end; it had invited it. The investigation would reveal that for the police force, the tragedy was not a shocking bolt from the blue, but a predictable inevitability. They had been told, repeatedly, that the caged vans were traps for the vulnerable and the distressed. They had chosen to look away, and in that dark, unmonitored metal box, the warnings turned into a statistic that finally forced the world to look at the emptiness for which the department was responsible."
